Where it began

Stuart Broad was born in Nottingham on 24 June 1986, the son of the England opener Chris Broad. At first he followed his father's lead and opened the batting. At sixteen he thought hockey might be his game, keeping goal for Leicestershire and the Midlands and earning a trial with an England age-group side.

Then, at seventeen, he grew, and the fast bowler appeared. He went to Oakham School, chose a contract with Leicestershire over a place at Durham University, and in 2006 the Cricket Writers' Club picked him as their Young Cricketer of the Year. In 2008 he moved to Nottinghamshire, his home county and his father's old club.

The player

His Test debut came in Colombo in December 2007, and he kept turning up for the next sixteen years. He played 167 Tests, the last in 2023, and took 604 wickets at 27.68, joining the small band of bowlers past 600. He had twenty five-wicket hauls and three ten-wicket matches.

The great days came in bunches. At The Oval in 2009 he took five wickets in an afternoon to help England regain the Ashes. In 2011 against India and in 2014 against Sri Lanka he took Test hat-tricks, the first Englishman to manage two; he only found out about the second when the public address announcer told him. And at Trent Bridge in 2015 he took eight for 15 on the first morning as Australia were bowled out for 60. No one had ever taken five Test wickets faster, and Wisden later named it the Test spell of the decade.

What made him special

Broad bowled in spells that felt like weather fronts: quiet for an hour, then a storm. When the mood took him, wickets fell in clusters. For years he shared the new ball with James Anderson, and the partnership became part of English summers.

He could bat too. In 2010 at Lord's he made 169 against Pakistan, sharing a world-record eighth-wicket stand of 332 with Jonathan Trott, and in doing so passed his father's best Test score. No father and son had both made Test hundreds for England before the Broads. Later on the runs came less often, and his final Test average was 18.04, but he never lost the knack of making a bowler work.

Away from the middle

He captained England in one-day and Twenty20 cricket, was part of the side that won the World Twenty20 in 2010, and was made a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and an MBE. After retiring he moved into the commentary box.

He went out in style. In his last Test, at The Oval in 2023, the last ball he faced went for six, and the last ball he bowled took the wicket that won the match.

And finally

In 2013 against New Zealand he batted for 103 minutes without scoring a run, at the time a Test record. This from the man who took the fastest five-wicket haul Test cricket had seen. Some days he simply preferred to do things at his own speed.
